💡 Key Takeaways
  • England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.
  • This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic.
  • The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

In a recent development, “I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”.

Industry observers note that avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

Recent findings suggest that it had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

In a recent development, it did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

It has been revealed that greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

Lauren James with a SUMPTUOUS finish but unfortunately it's offside 🥹 Watch Greece v England on ITV1 📺 https://t.co/4s9neVKIaR.

Sources indicate that ioanna Papatheodorou nearly gave Greece the lead when she dribbled past Esme Morgan and Leah Williamson with ease but her powerful strike hit the crossbar. It was a let-off for England, but they made it count by taking the lead just before half-time.

Industry observers note that A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

According to recent reports, who else but Georgia Stanway?! 👏 A slick move and finish sees England ahead in Crete 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 @Lionesses | @ITV https://t.co/cdfFKODxSp.

Le Tissier scored England’s second just past the hour mark before Alessia Russo made it 3-0 four minutes later. It appeared the floodgates may have opened but that proved to be a false dawn, with Greece scoring a deserved goal through Kallisti Brouksair after some poor England defending.

Maya Le Tissier's FIRST goal for England 🙌 The @ManUtdWomen defender finishes with aplomb 💥 https://t.co/pF8MQKXfIa.

It has been revealed that while this game will go down as largely forgettable, it will be remembered by 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson and Grace Fisk, 28, who came on for their senior debuts in the closing stages. It also means Parkinson, who could have played for Japan, Portugal or Singapore, is now tied to England.

She is an exciting player for the future but will feel she has a chance of making a World Cup squad, should England get there. For now, they are taking the slow route.

Greece (4-3-3) Petaloti; Giannaka, Gkouni, Markou, Paterna; Drakogiannaki (Kongouli, 78), Brame (Saich, 68), Moraitou (Chalatsogianni, 68); Sarri (Tzourtzevits, 87), Papathedorou, Brouksair.Goal Brouksair (77).Subs not used Giannkouli, Katergiannaki, Ntarzanou, Theodoraki, Kapnisi, Rapani, Pouliou, Tsela.

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”.

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman stated. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

Recent findings suggest that “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

According to recent reports, all eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”.

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”.

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 15:04 EST, 17 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino’s whirlwind arrival as Manchester United’s upcoming head coach has left little time to work out where he will live – but a key factor in that decision will be his beloved dog Sansa.

Pochettino will leave the TQL Stadium in Cincinnati after the USA’s game against Haiti in the early hours of Wednesday morning and go straight to the airport to catch an eight-hour flight to Manchester on board a private jet paid for by United.

The club will also provide him with somewhere to live as he settles into the new job and finds a more permanent residence.

The 54-year-old, who also has a home in Barcelona, is said to have lived just outside London when he was Tottenham manager and then spent the entirety of his 18-month spell as Paris Saint-Germain boss in a luxury hotel.

Pochettino lived in Knightsbridge while he was in charge of Chelsea, and revealed that he enjoyed getting feedback from fans while out on his daily 90-minute dog walks with Sansa.

He named the Rhodesian Ridgeback after a character from Game of Thrones and has even given the dog her own Instagram account.

Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of the US national team for the final time in the early hours of Wednesday morning, then head straight to Manchester on a private jet.

Pochettino (pictured with his son Maurizio) will have to find accommodation which suits his dog Sansa, a Rhodesian Ridgeback (Source: Instagram/pochettino).

Describing the difficulty of Spurs playing on a Saturday night in 2018, he mentioned: ‘At 7pm, I am normally on my sofa with my dog Sansa watching the Spanish league because they start at 7.45pm, or France because Ligue 1 starts at 8pm, or Italy, or different games.

‘It will be so strange for my dog. Not for me but my dog. “Where is my dad?” she is going to say. She is beautiful and I am in love with her.’.

According to recent reports, the living habits of United bosses have varied over the years. Sir Alex Ferguson, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and Ruben Amorim favoured Wilmslow and Alderley Edge, David Moyes remained further afield in Lytham, Louis van Gaal and Erik ten Hag chose Hale, and Jose Mourinho famously spent 895 days at the Lowry Hotel in Manchester (where dogs can stay for an additional £30).

United have no aims to change the timings for Wednesday’s training session, even though Pochettino and four of his backroom team may not arrive at Carrington until the early afternoon.

The private jet carrying the Argentine, first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott should touch down from Cincinnati around noon.

An advance party of three more coaches – Pochettino’s assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, and his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino – have been in Manchester since Sunday after they were released early by the US Soccer Federation as a gesture of goodwill following the 6-0 first-leg win over Haiti in the quarter-finals of the North American equivalent of the Nations League.

They took training on Tuesday as United’s players continue to report back from international duty, and will also oversee the session on Wednesday morning after United decided not to reschedule it so Pochettino could be present.

The Argentine will be firmly hands-on from Thursday, though, as he prepares for his first game against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

Pochettino, who will speak to club media shortly after his arrival before conducting his first press conference on Friday, has faced Liverpool 19 times in his managerial career, losing 11 games, drawing five and winning three.

Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez (right) has been in Manchester since Sunday and took training on Tuesday.

Strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya - the first woman to be part of United's backroom staff - will travel with Pochettino to Manchester following the Haiti game.

Pochettino will inherit a team in the relegation zone – which could even be bottom of the Premier League by kick-off on Sunday – and it’s understood he will be given modest funds to improve his squad in the January transfer window.

United are in desperate need of a left back and a striker, having failed to sign cover in both positions in the summer.

According to recent reports, one potential target may be US centre forward Folarin Balogun who has prospered under Pochettino but only started once for Monaco this season after a summer move to Everton fell through. United sources say the new head coach will have input in the weeks ahead before a clearer initiative emerges.

United also want a centre back after Confidential revealed last week that Fulham’s Calvin Bassey and Nathan Collins, of Brentford, are two options being considered.

It’s possible that one of those deals may have to be a loan, however, with United’s delicate financial situation set to be spelt out in black and white when the results from the first quarter of the financial year are released on Thursday.

Although Pochettino is going to have money for newly introduced players, United will have to be smart in their transfer dealings and spend wisely.

In the short term, Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford may be available again for the first time in more than a month against Liverpool.

However, there is a concern over Patrick Dorgu who was deemed to be unfit for international duty with Denmark, even though he returned to action for Michael Carrick’s final game after a month-and-a-half out with a hamstring injury and headed a stoppage-time equaliser in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa.

Fulham's Calvin Bassey (right) is among the centre-back options United are considering.

Marcus Rashford may be available for the first time in more than a month against Liverpool.

It was the departure of Travis Binnion, rather than Carrick, that raised the most eyebrows among figures working in football over the past few days.

Agents and first-team players privately described their surprise at seeing Binnion – a long-time academy figure before stepping up to the first team to help Darren Fletcher as interim and then Carrick – leave the club.

United have cleaned house for the arrival of Pochettino’s backroom team, and Binnion was one of those who paid the price.

A popular figure in the dressing room, Joshua Zirkzee, Benjamin Sesko and Kobbie Mainoo are among the players who are known to have enjoyed working with Binnion.

Despite stepping up to the first team, where he would watch matches from the press box alongside United’s team of analysts, Binnion remained in contact with numerous academy player representatives to ensure their development was progressing as planned.

Binnion, who first arrived in 2019 as an Under 16s coach and progressed to the Under 18s, Under 21s and then head of player development and coaching, isn’t expected to be out of the game for too long though.

Sources indicate that agency sources believe rival Premier League academies will move rapidly to recruit him, with Everton seen as one potential landing spot. United’s former academy head Nick Cox is now Everton technical director and has already recruited Dave Hughes and Tom Curtis, who worked under Binnion at United.

A popular figure in the dressing room, Joshua Zirkzee, Benjamin Sesko and Kobbie Mainoo are among the players who enjoyed working with Travis Binnion (pictured).

Your responses to our 36-man Manchester United squad audit have made for interesting reading over the last week.

Confidential pored over the first-team squad, as well as numerous rising stars in the academy, that Pochettino and his staff will quickly have to run the rule over.

While some of the voting went as expected – your votes demonstrated an overwhelming desire among the fanbase to see Noussair Mazraoui, Diogo Dalot, Shaw and Harry Maguire leave this summer – there were a few surprises.

Many voted for captain Bruno Fernandes, who just recently rejected a second contract extension offer, to be moved on, along with Rashford. Amad Diallo and summer signing Andrey Santos are two who divide opinion, but both made the cut.

Check out the full squad audit HERE to see how others voted and leave your own verdict!

Confidential understands JJ Gabriel’s representatives held fresh talks with Real Madrid at the club’s training ground on Monday as a move to the Santiago Bernabeu edges ever closer.

Now that Gabriel has officially unveiled a partnership with Epic Sports Agency, his agent Ali Barat is leading negotiations and has been at Real’s Valdebebas headquarters along with the 16-year-old and his family.

Gabriel announced his departure from the club in an Instagram video on Tuesday night, as he and the Spanish giants hope to get a move over the line.

JJ Gabriel's representatives have held fresh talks with Real Madrid as his move to the Bernabeu edges closer.

Eric Cantona and Sir Alex Ferguson will reunite next month at a special screening of the Frenchman’s new documentary.

Cantona: Flower of Evil won rave reviews in France and is now heading to the UK, with a one-night-only panel featuring Cantona and Ferguson at Aviva Studios in Manchester on December 7.

It has been revealed that the documentary film digs deeper into how Ferguson channelled Cantona’s brilliance and honed his explosiveness – a trait that had seen him branded ‘unmanageable’ in France. Tickets range from £156 all the way up to £1,000. You can purchase them here.

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 11:34, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 11:34.

Everton manager David Moyes has confirmed that Jack Grealish is back available for Monday's Premier League showdown with Brentford at the Gtech Community Stadium.

The Manchester City loanee has missed the Toffees' last four games in all competitions due to a breach of club discipline, but he returned to action in a friendly during the international break.

Grealish has since been welcomed back to team training and is an option for gameweek 11, but the winger will surely be on the bench at best after a few weeks with no competitive minutes.

Instead, Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George should be retained in the wide areas, providing support to the two main men in Thierno Barry and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall.

Barry registered his fifth, sixth and seventh Premier League goal involvements of the season last time out, scoring two of his own and setting up Dewsbury-Hall in Everton's 3-1 win over Coventry City, but only two of his strikes have come on the road.

Further back, Harrison Armstrong and James Garner are midfield mainstays, while Moyes also has no reason to alter a backline that has conceded just five away goals this season.

Jordan Pickford's status as England number one may now be in question thanks to James Trafford's exploits, but the 32-year-old remains Moyes's undisputed first pick.

Everton possible starting lineup:.

Pickford; Rohl, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong; Dibling, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry.

  • This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

The human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

It has been revealed that intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Industry observers note that here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

In a recent development, to model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).

Recent findings suggest that to characterize the morphology, cellular composition and patterning of the epithelium, we developed a 3D-printed ‘histomold’ for simultaneous embedding and perpendicular sectioning of up to 50 engineered epithelia (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and mIF staining highlighted histological and cell-type patterning similarity to donor-matched primary tissue (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Figs. 1g and 2a–c). In addition, a duodenal dual reporter line stably labelling chromatin (H2BC4–mTurquoise2) and LGR5+ stem cells (LGR5–IRES-NLS-mScarlet3) confirmed LGR5 ISC localization to the crypt bottom (Fig. 1f). By day 10, the thick epithelium contained proliferative SOX9+ and Ki67+ cells primarily confined to the crypt, whereas mature enterocytes (APOA4+ in the duodenum, and FABP6+ in the ileum) and colonocytes (CA1+) were enriched within inter-crypt regions (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3a–f), with αDEF5+ Paneth cells detected in some small intestinal crypts (Extended Data Fig. 3g). EdU pulse-chase labelling revealed that cycling cells, initially localized in the crypt base, progressively migrated towards the apical surface over 4 days, similar to homeostatic turnover in vivo11 (Extended Data Fig. 3h and Supplementary Video 1). These data confirm that imposing in vivo-inspired geometries on human intestinal organoids drives reproducible cell-type regionalization and migration akin to the intestinal crypt–villus axis9.

Multiplexed scRNA-seq demonstrated region-specific stem, absorptive and secretory lineages across seven donors at day 10 (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Cell-type composition was similar to primary tissue counterparts and proportions were consistent across donors, highlighting the fidelity and robustness of the system (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Gene Ontology analysis of enterocyte and colonocyte marker genes revealed enrichment of distinct physiological programs concordant with the primary intestinal regions12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Proximal small intestinal enterocytes indicated higher expression of genes involving lipid, xenobiotic and iron metabolism (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Pseudotemporal ordering of the duodenal stem-to-enterocyte trajectory confirmed enterocyte maturation levels, approaching the AQP10+ expression observed at the villus tip in vivo14 (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Distal small intestinal enterocytes expressed bile acid and vitamin B12 transport genes, whereas colonocytes were enriched in cell–cell interactions and ion transport13,15 (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We confirmed differential protein expression of the transporters SLC5A1, SLC10A2 and SLC26A2 between the regions (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Among secretory lineages, enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells were differentially abundant, with substantial heterogeneity in enteroendocrine cells (CHGA+) including EC (TPH1+), MX (GHRL+ and MLN+), D (SST+), K (GIP+), I (CCK+) and L (GCG+ and PYY+) subpopulations that match tissue distribution16 (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 4g–j).

Collectively, these data show that the engineered epithelium retains region-specific cell composition, spatial organization and gene expression, providing inroads to explore nutrient, xenobiotic and host–microbe processes in a human context.

In a recent development, the mucus, a layered network of mucins, cellular material, antimicrobials and structural factors, provides an interactive barrier between the microbiome and intestinal epithelium. Characterizing the properties and functional role of the mucus at the host–microbe interface remains largely under-explored in vitro. To facilitate rapid accumulation of mucus, we reduced the apical volume over the course of approximately 4 days, which resulted in a fibrous mucus network covering the epithelium (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). Shed cells were present throughout the mucus layer, where they contribute to viscosity17 and can exert an antimicrobial role18 (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Longitudinal sections revealed an irregular mucus profile, with higher colonic thickness and crypt plumes similar to observations in primary tissue19 (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). AlcianBlue–Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) co-staining showed regional differences in secretion and glycosylation, with higher ratios of acidic, negatively charged groups towards colon (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). These patterns were comparable with the primary tissue and may be influenced by relative levels of fucose, sialic acid and sulfate groups20. Proteomic analysis of the colonic luminal content identified the core mucus layer proteins21 (MUC2, FCGBP, TFF3, AGR2, CLCA1, ZG16 and MUC5B) as major constituents, alongside additional mucins, antimicrobials and lectin-binding proteins (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 5j and Supplementary Table 5). Using the scRNA-seq data, we identified seven non-proliferative (MKI67−) goblet cell clusters (C0–C6) representing regional diversity and differentiation state (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 5k and Supplementary Table 3). Colonic goblet cells (C1) were enriched in intracellular vesicle transport, protein glycosylation and aerobic respiration, suggesting a higher secretion machinery consistent with thickness measurements (Extended Data Fig. 5l and Supplementary Table 4).

Next, we benchmarked the expression of membrane-bound mucins, key glycocalyx components that fortify the epithelium but remain difficult to recapitulate in vitro22. We observed a strong cell-type and region-specific gene expression comparable with the reference tissue (Fig. 2i). MUC6 and MUC5AC, which encode stomach mucins that are often expressed under pathological and metaplastic conditions23,24, were nearly absent. MUC12 and MUC17 staining in the engineered epithelium and tissue counterparts confirmed the specificity and maturation of the glycocalyx, revealing in vivo-like levels by day 12 of culture (Fig. 2j,k and Extended Data Fig. 5m). Finally, we functionally assessed the mucus upon colonization with the commensals Enterococcus faecium or Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, which proliferated without compromising epithelial integrity (Fig. 2l and Extended Data Fig. 5n). Together, these results indicate that the platform can accumulate a complex mucus layer with in vivo-like and region-specific properties, opening fresh avenues for the study of human mucus and host–microbe interactions.

Unlike commensal microbiota, the foodborne pathogen S.Tm exploits motility and adhesion mechanisms to penetrate the mucus25, triggering an invasion-dependent inflammatory response that facilitates pathogen colonization26. Although extensive research has characterized the fundamental mechanisms underlying S.Tm infection, the exact epithelial responses and the resulting epithelial–immune signalling remain unresolved at the human level and at single-cell resolution.

In a recent development, motivated by the higher mucus level and its potential role against pathogenic bacteria, we infected colonic epithelium with S.Tm 14028 in conditions with varying densities of mucus. At 18 h post-start of the infection (hpi), S.Tm triggered strong damage in conditions with less mucus (Mucuslo), whereas the epithelium remained largely unaffected in the presence of dense mucus (Mucushi; Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Furthermore, the denser mucus led to a decrease in microbial burden, cell invasion and cytokine release, while preserving barrier integrity (Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). These protective effects were coupled with cell shedding, which predominantly localized at crypt openings, presumably impeding bacterial colonization (Extended Data Fig. 6h).

According to recent reports, next, we used single-cell transcriptome and accessible chromatin sequencing (scMultiome) to characterize the Mucushi colonic epithelium response at 24 hpi and epithelial breach (Extended Data Fig. 6i). We detected canonical cell types in control and S.Tm conditions with increased proportion of mature colonocytes upon infection, a shift reported in mouse tissue27 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6j–l). Of note, ‘colonocyte subtype 1’ (RNA clusters C7-1 and C7-2) and ‘subtype 2’ (RNA cluster C8) were nearly exclusive to the infection condition (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6k). Overall, all cell types exhibited a pronounced response to infection with 3,056 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 34,337 differentially accessible open chromatin regions (DARs) between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6m–p and Supplementary Table 3). Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted hypoxia, NF-κB and barrier or cytoskeletal signatures, including upregulation of antimicrobials (LCN2 and PIGR), reactive oxygen species (DUOX2 and DUOXA2) and inflammatory cytokines (CCL20, IL18 and IL32; Extended Data Fig. 6q–s). Stem cells strongly upregulated LCN2, chemokines (CXCL1–3) and immunomodulators (TNF and LTB). Together, these results identify a complex innate epithelium response involving sensing, barrier maintenance and mucosal signalling.

Industry observers note that we used the chromatin accessibility data to infer a gene regulatory network underlying the epithelial response (Fig. 3g). This network revealed transcription factor nodes and target genes that orchestrate a broad-spectrum response, along with clusters that specifically coordinate infection-specific states. We identified BHLHE40, ZNF292 and RBPJ as the top differentially expressed transcription factors in the colonocyte subtype 1, which exhibited a hypoxic signature that appears conserved under infections and inflammatory-related diseases28. STAT3 emerged as a central node of the colonocyte subtype 2. Phosphorylation of STAT3 (pSTAT3) has been linked to intracellular S.Tm infection29 via the virulence factor SteE30,31, leading to an anti-inflammatory transcriptional program that supports the bacterial niche. Co-staining of pSTAT3 and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) revealed a strong colocalization both in colonic and small intestinal samples, with no pSTAT3 detection in non-infected conditions (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). These results, in addition to the expression of the STAT3 negative-feedback regulator SOCS3, suggest that this population is S.Tm specific and contains cells with intracellular bacteria.

In a recent development, finally, we classified DEGs into co-expression gene modules based on expression differences across cell types between conditions (Supplementary Table 3). We found that the colonocyte subtype 2-specific gene module exhibited increased reactive oxygen species, endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response and ferroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 7d and Supplementary Table 4). Furthermore, we observed a possible antagonistic interaction between host cell and pathogen, with non-cannonical inflammasome signalling (CASP4, CASP5 and IL18)32 and genes with anti-inflammatory roles (SBNO2 and TNIP3; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). BACH1, a key oxidative stress and ferroptosis regulator competing with NRF2 (NFE2L2)33,34, was also among the top upregulated transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Binding motifs of STAT3 and BACH1 were over-represented in S.Tm DARs, indicating that both might be regulators of this population (Supplementary Table 6). Finally, we identified putative gene regulatory regions with increased accessibility upon infection, including intronic and distal regions of IL18 and SLC7A11 in the presumably invaded cells (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 7h). Collectively, these findings identify a complex multipartite human epithelial gene regulatory response to S.Tm infection, confirm STAT3 activation in S.Tm-invaded cells, and demonstrate how engineered intestines can be used to illuminate human infection responses.

In a recent development, central to S.Tm pathogenesis resides a specialized virulence machinery including two needle-like type III secretion systems (T3SS-1/2) that mediate invasion and intracellular survival26,35 (Fig. 3j). To study how virulence factors influence the host response to luminal and intracellular S.Tm, we performed short, high-load infections (approximately 3 h, multiplicity of infection of approximately 1:60, −mucus) using wild-type (WT) and mutant strains. Subsequent gentamicin treatment removed the luminal stimulus while maintaining intracellular S.Tm populations for several days (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

We observed that flagellum-driven motility (ΔfliC–ΔfljB (ΔFg)) contributed more to invasion than SiiE-dependent adhesion (ΔsiiF; Extended Data Fig. 8b). Consistent with our previous results (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c), internalized S.Tm predominantly localized basolaterally beneath the nucleus, presumably within Salmonella-containing vacuoles (SCV)35 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Intracellular replication led to either cell extrusion events with luminal release or rupture of SCV-like structures that released S.Tm basally (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Videos 2 and 3). The levels of IL-18 increased over 96 hpi and was a hallmark with WT but not avirulent ΔinvG–ΔssaV (ΔSPI-1/2) S.Tm, distinguishing this invasion signature from the broader luminal cytokine response (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). In addition, the system demonstrated virulence sensitivity, as S.Tm SL1344 (ref. 36) elicited an exacerbated invasion-driven response marked by increased internalization, cell shedding and IL-18 secretion compared with S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 8g).

To resolve host transcriptional responses induced by luminal or intracellular S.Tm, we performed scRNA-seq on GFP+ (invaded (In)) and GFP− (non-invaded (Out)) cells infected with WTGFP, ΔSPI-1/2GFP, ΔssaVGFP (ΔSPI-2) or ΔsteEGFP strains at 24 hpi (Fig. 3j,l and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Invasion occurred across all cell types but was lowest in stem cells, probably given their crypt-base localization (Extended Data Fig. 8j). The luminal response of non-invaded (GFP−) colonocytes was comparable between WT and ΔSPI-1/2, involving hypoxia, barrier and cytokine genes (Fig. 3m). A low-abundant colonocyte state appeared independent of invasion and was marked by IFN signalling (MX1 and ISG15), probably reflecting extracellular bacterial recognition37 (Fig. 3m, ‘depleted non-infected’, Extended Data Fig. 8i and Supplementary Table 4). The intracellular response of invaded (GFP+) colonocytes, which matched the colonocyte subtype 2 state from the multiomic analysis, triggered a profound shift (approximately 4,000 DEGs) characterized by pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory, bacterial recognition, cytoskeleton and oxidative stress genes with variable patterns along differentiation (Fig. 3m, Extended Data Fig. 8k,l and Supplementary Table 2). Although effector contributions may differ functionally, the attenuated gene signature observed in ΔSPI-2, and especially in ΔsteE-invaded cells, positions SteE as a key driver of the intracellular transcriptional landscape (‘enriched in GFP+’; Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8i,l,m).

Among transcription factors, STAT3 (STAT3, SOCS3 and pSTAT3) was attenuated in ΔSPI-2 and absent in ΔsteE-invaded cells, confirming its SteE-mediated activation31 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,n). Invasion by WT and mutants elicited coordinated upregulation of the antagonistic BACH1–NRF2 transcription factor pair33 that coincided with reduced expression of iron homeostasis regulators (GPX4, FTH1, HMOX1 and FTL), suggesting predominant BACH1 activity34 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,o). SLC7A11 was a notable exception to this repression, possibly through non-canonical BACH1 activation34, STAT3 regulation38 or an alternative mechanism. Although the exact BACH1–NRF2 interplay and roles remain to be fully elucidated, these transcription factors appeared functionally coupled to intracellular S.Tm, as observed upon small-molecule inhibitor treatments (Extended Data Fig. 8p).

Recent findings suggest that finally, we classified S.TmWT-invaded cells by bacterial burden using imaging flow cytometry, identifying single-colony to high-load groups at 24 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 8q). To link intracellular replication levels to host response, we performed single-cell total RNA sequencing (VASA-seq) on index-sorted cells from GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi levels (Extended Data Fig. 8r). GFPhi cells, with up to 35 colony-forming units (CFU) per cell, most strongly correlated with our previously defined intracellular gene module, linking the host response to S.Tm activity and replication rather than invasion alone (Extended Data Fig. 8s,t). Uniquely, VASA-seq recovered not only non-protein coding host transcripts but also bacterial genes involved in metabolism (mgtB, gltA and feoB) and SPI-2 machinery, highlighting the intracellular adaptation of the pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 8u,v and Supplementary Table 3). Collectively, these data provide a high-resolution, multi-modal atlas that uncovers how virulence factors and intracellular burden shape the invaded epithelial response.

Industry observers note that our transcriptomic analysis identified epithelial signals triggered by S.Tm infection and confirmed the epithelium as a sensor of pathogen presence. Elucidating the functional impact of these signals requires the presence of their target populations. Given that S.Tm infection was associated with induction of lymphocyte-targeting cytokines (IL-18 and TNF) and chemokines (CXCL10 and CCL20), we focused on T cells as putative responders and introduced them into the intestinal engineered tissues. In the human intestine, TRM cells reside within the mucosa to safeguard barrier integrity39. We have previously demonstrated that TRM cells integrate into ISC-derived organoids and respond to synthetic T cell receptor (TCR) engagement40. Building on this approach, we established immunosurveilled barriers by incorporating autologous tissue-resident immune cells into the ECM scaffold of our engineered tissues (Fig. 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). These cells were isolated primarily from the small intestine due to higher proximal mucosal immune cell density5. We first assessed immune cell interactions with the epithelium, in the absence of a pathogenic threat. As expected from their tissue-resident phenotype facilitating epithelial interaction (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h), intraepithelial lymphocytes infiltrated the epithelium at physiological rates and patrolling speeds comparable with the organ of origin41 without compromising barrier integrity (Fig. 4d–i, Extended Data Fig. 9i,j and Supplementary Videos 4–6). By contrast, blood-derived T cells barely integrated into the epithelium (Fig. 4f).

To resolve the cellular diversity and epithelium–immune crosstalk, we performed scRNA-seq after 1 week of co-culture. The immune compartment exhibited striking heterogeneity, comprising CD8 T (CD8 TRM) cells, CD4 T helper (CD4 TRM) cells, regulatory T cells, T helper 17 (TH17 TRM) cells, γδ T cells, natural killer cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and memory B cells (Fig. 4j), demonstrating maintenance of immune lineage fidelity (Extended Data Fig. 9k). TRM populations constituted the majority of the immune cell pool, remaining non-proliferative, consistent with their long-lived quiescent state in vivo42 (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 9d–g,k). Given their dominant representation, we refer to the entire immune compartment as ‘TRM cells’ henceforth. Although overall epithelial cell-type composition was unaffected (Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 9l,m), immune cell presence induced epithelial antigen processing and presentation programs, marked by upregulation of MHC class I (MHC-I) components (HLA-B and B2M) and the MHC-II chaperone CD74 (Fig. 4l, Extended Data Fig. 9n–p and Supplementary Table 4). Transcription factor expression analysis in the enterocyte cluster linked gene expression changes to STAT1, IRF1 and IRF9, canonical hallmarks of IFNγ signalling (Fig. 4l), suggesting that immune-derived IFNγ facilitates this baseline immune priming43 (Fig. 4m). We confirmed IFNγ within culture supernatants at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 9q).

Sources indicate that next, we found that engineered tissues recapitulate key epithelial–immune interactions, including IFNGR1/2–IFNG, IL15RA–IL15 (ref. 44) and TNFRSF14–CD160 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4m and Supplementary Table 7). Furthermore, introduction of resident immune cells drove upregulation of the butyrophilin-like (BTNL) molecules BTNL3 and BTNL8 within the epithelium, probably in a HNF4G-dependent manner46 (Fig. 4l). These epithelial BTNL molecules signal back to the immune compartment, facilitating maturation of Vγ4+ γδ T cells and establishing a protective mucosal circuit, whose disruption is linked to intestinal pathology47.

Together, these data suggest that engineered intestinal tissues preserve physiological immune cell behaviours and foster in vivo-like epithelial–immune interactions.

Having incorporated TRM cells into the engineered tissues, we next asked how they interpret epithelial-derived signals to orchestrate mucosal defence upon S.Tm infection. We challenged immunocompetent barriers with high-load S.Tm for 3 h following gentamicin treatment (Fig. 5a). Histological analysis confirmed bacteria within close proximity of intraepithelial lymphocytes (Fig. 5b). The presence of resident immune cells accelerated mucosal damage compared with epithelium-only controls, leading to increased epithelial shedding and loss of barrier integrity (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). Attributing elevated epithelial damage to TRM cell activation, we analysed the basal compartment for inflammatory mediators observed in patients with gastroenteric Salmonella infection48,49. We identified two temporally distinct regimes of immune and epithelial responses. A rapid (10 hpi) first wave of IL-2 and IFNγ secretion, indicating a canonical CD4+ TH1 response, occurred concurrently with epithelial secretion of IL-18 (Fig. 5d). This initial response was followed by release of cytotoxic and antimicrobial effectors, including GzmB, IL-6 and TH17-associated cytokines (IL17A and IL-22). TNF, IL-13 and IL-1β were modestly induced (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). Although facilitating pathogen clearance (Extended Data Fig. 10f), this TH1–TH17-driven TRM cell response was associated with mucosal injury.

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether TRM cell activation requires epithelial invasion or only luminal exposure to the pathogen, we leveraged the S.Tm mutants introduced previously (ΔFg, ΔSPI-2 and ΔSPI-1/2; Fig. 3). We found that the extent of mucosal injury and the magnitude of TRM cell response correlated with S.Tm invasive capacity and epithelial IL-18 secretion (Fig. 5e,f and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Furthermore, in line with the stronger epithelial response described earlier (Extended Data Fig. 8g), S.Tm SL1344 induced a more rapid and severe immunopathology than S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 10h). Together, these data link TRM cell responses to pathogen virulence, invasive capacity and subsequent epithelial cytokine secretion. Although TRM cell responses are classically defined by antigen-specific TCRs, their capacity for innate-like bystander responses is a critical yet poorly understood feature of human mucosal immunity. We sought to understand whether S.Tm-mediated TRM cell activation is driven by secreted epithelial signals rather than direct TCR binding to epithelial MHC. Inhibition of PI3K and p38 MAPK, essential for innate-like IFNγ induction50, significantly quelled the response, whereas TCR-dependent LCK inhibition51 showed no effect (Fig. 5g). Likewise, surface TCR expression remained stable during S.Tm infection, contrasting the expected downregulation triggered by synthetic TCR engagement via an EpCAM–CD3 bispecific52 (Fig. 5h). Conditioned media from infected epithelium-only barriers were sufficient to activate TRM cells, whereas direct stimulation with bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (LPS and flagellin) failed to trigger degranulation (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10i). We note that this non-cognate response appeared to be a hallmark of tissue residency, as allogeneic and autologous blood-derived T cells remained unresponsive to infection, despite exhibiting substantial CD45RO+ populations (Extended Data Fig. 9d), high viability and IL-2 induction capacity (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these results establish S.Tm-induced TRM cell activation in this system as a TCR-independent bystander response that requires inflammatory signals relayed by the epithelium. The induction of IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion closely coincided with the kinetics of the T cell response (Fig. 5d), implicating this cytokine as a key epithelial orchestrator of T cell activation. This was supported by high expression of IL-18Rα on CD4+ TRM cells, which conferred pronounced responsiveness to exogenous IL-18 and S.Tm infection (Fig. 5j and Extended Data Fig. 10l,m). To assess its role as an epithelial messenger, we generated IL18 knockouts in intestinal organoids using CRISPR–Cas9, resulting in ablation of IL-18 expression at baseline and upon challenge (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 10n). Indeed, IL-18 levels in WT S.Tm-infected mutant barriers were comparable with those of the avirulent ΔSPI-1/2 infection and non-infected control (Fig. 5l). When assessing the TRM cell response, IL-18 deficiency significantly dampened the inflammatory response (Fig. 5l,m), attenuating intracellular IFNγ levels in the cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ responder population (Extended Data Fig. 10o). Critically, the loss of IL-18 protected the barrier from pathological shedding and thinning (Fig. 5n and Extended Data Fig. 10p) despite functional T cell responder potential, linking IL-18-driven T cell activation to immunopathology.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the epithelium orchestrates antibacterial mucosal defence by secreting IL-18 to trigger non-cognate, innate-like responses of the TRM compartment.

We have reported bioengineered, luminally accessible human intestinal tissues comprising epithelia with periodically repeating crypts that maintain LGR5+ stem cells, in vivo-like cell composition and patterning, and retain transcriptomic signatures across multiple donors. Identical medium and biophysical culture conditions yield region-specific signatures due to stem cell origin. Cell-type maturation and a reduction in total apical volume enable the formation of a region-specific mucus layer with mature glycocalyx. In addition, autologous TRM cells patrol the barrier and engage in bidirectional crosstalk with the epithelium, conferring an immune-responsive state within epithelial cells via IFNγ signalling.

It has been revealed that the modularity of the system enabled newly introduced inquiry into S.Tm infection in a human context, contributing to collective efforts to refine physiologically relevant enteric infection models53. Basolateral S.Tm localization within polarized cells presumably facilitates dissemination into the lamina propria, a phenomenon that has been reported in vivo54,55. In addition, the phenotypic divergence observed between SL1344 and 14028 strains could expand to clinical isolates and human-restricted pathogens (for example, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi, Shigella flexneri and Vibrio cholerae), including the study of host factors influencing bacterial gene expression and antibiotic susceptibility. We mapped the gene regulatory networks underlying luminal and intracellular S.Tm at single-cell resolution. The epithelium orchestrated inflammatory, metabolic and structural responses that accompany S.Tm colonization26 and demonstrate an innate-sensing capacity that coordinates multi-lineage immune recruitment in vivo. S.Tm invasion reshaped the host transcriptome through a SteE-dependent STAT3 gene regulatory hub that extends results in macrophages and immortalized lines29,31. The reduced SPI-2 contribution may stem from non-transcriptional effector roles or delayed activation resulting from the SPI-1-inducing pre-culture protocol56. In addition, changes in oxidative stress and iron homeostasis suggest a host–pathogen interplay associated with other intracellular infections57, warranting further study. Overall, these responses were highly influenced by the intracellular burden of the pathogen.

Advancing our previous work40 to an apically accessible immunocompetent system, we demonstrated that epithelial IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion is sufficient to drive TRM cell activation and cytokine release, reflecting clinical gastroenteric salmonellosis48,49. The system allowed us to elucidate the functional effects of this bystander T cell activation, aligning with previous reports of innate-like polyfunctional capabilities of TRM cells58,59,60. TRM cells intensified infection-mediated epithelial shedding, which probably contributes to pathogen clearance61 and is consistent with the rapid onset of diarrhoea during S.Tm infection. Although mouse studies have established the necessity of IL-18 for CD4+ T cell defence upon S.Tm infection62, it has been shown that enteric neurons, rather than the epithelium, serve as the critical source of IL-18 for intestinal protection63. We demonstrated that the human intestinal epithelium can potently activate TRM cells via IL-18 to drive defence responses, at least in an in vitro setting. Of note, S.Tm infection64 and IL-18 (ref. 65) have been linked to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. Our data raise the possibility that this association may be underpinned by the appearance of a cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ T cell population58,62.

Although our platform provides a unique window into human intestinal in vitro modelling, several limitations remain. The engineered tissues lack villous structures, specialized Paneth or M cells, and myeloid immune lineages, crucial mediators of immunity against infection. The lack of fluid exchange might affect biophysical characteristics of a mucus layer accumulated by apical media reduction. Furthermore, S.Tm invasion rates probably exceed physiological levels due to mucus protection. Future studies may circumvent these limitations through bioengineering approaches9, mucus secretagogues, cytokine supplementation or the inclusion of additional commensal and immune lineages.

It has been revealed that beyond host–pathogen interaction, the engineered tissues and analytical framework expand what can be addressed ex vivo. The mature, patterned epithelium opens research directions in region-specific drugs and nutrient absorption, mucus biology and epithelial–TRM cell interactions implicated in inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis. Overall, the platform brings the field closer to capturing complex, organ-level processes in a human setting that is controllable and tractable.

Industry observers note that during the work on this project, a large number of microdevice prototype versions were fabricated using a range of microfabrication techniques, including cleanroom soft lithography, 3D printing, two-photon polymerization (2PP) lithography, computer numerical control (CNC) milling and plastic injection molding. The final chip is designed in a slide format (75 × 25 mm) containing three independent chips per slide. Each chip contained a central hydrogel chamber flanked by two side medium reservoirs and one top medium reservoir. The hydrogel precursor was injected through a loading port leading to the central gel chamber. A cylindrical stamp with a microtopography (for example, an array of biomimetic micropillars) on its base was placed onto a stamp-holding edge of the top reservoir before gel injection. After gel polymerization (see details in a separate section), the stamp was removed, leaving an inverse microtopography (for example, an array of microwells) on the hydrogel surface. The top and side reservoirs were then filled with PBS or cell culture medium. The top reservoir was used for cell seeding and subsequently served as the apical medium reservoir after epithelial coverage of the hydrogel and barrier formation. Medium from the side reservoirs passively diffused through the gel, supplying the epithelial tissue with nutrients from the basal side. Early prototypes were fabricated using conventional soft lithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) molding workflows established at the Center of Micronanotechnology (EPFL). The 3D chip design was split into two photomasks that were sequentially aligned to enable the creation of pseudo-3D features and different heights for phase-guiding micro-pillars. Chip layouts were patterned onto chrome-coated fused silica substrates via laser lithography (VPG200, Heidelberg Instruments). Three layers of SU8 GM1075 (Gerlteltec) were sequentially spin coated onto dehydrated silicon wafers to achieve a total mold thickness of 750 μm. The first two 250-μm layers were soft baked, exposed to UV through the first photomask (MA6/BA6, Süss MicroTec) and post-baked. Then, the third SU8 layer was spin coated, soft baked and the second photomask was aligned to the existing pattern using dedicated alignment marks. After a final post-exposure bake and development with propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA; Sigma), the molds were hard baked at 135 °C for 4 h and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was mixed at a 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio, poured onto the molds, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 24 h. PDMS replicas were cut, punched and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. The strength of the soft lithography pipeline is in fabrication of high-resolution microfeatures and with relatively optimal throughput, as 10–20 chips can be produced from a single wafer. However, fabrication of the models taller than 500 μm is challenging and only step-like, pseudo-3D features from a single side of the PDMS layer can be fabricated. To overcome these limitations, we explored several other complementary fabrication strategies. Commercial 3D-printing techniques such as fused deposition modelling and stereolithography were used for the production of larger models (Formlabs Form 4). However, these methods lacked the resolution and surface finish required for high-quality PDMS molding and were suitable only for some early-stage proof-of-concept prototypes. Instead, here we used 2PP lithography using the UpNano NanoOne printer to fabricate detailed 3D features of the chip. In brief, 3D models of the microchip were created in Autodesk Fusion (latest version), exported as STL files and processed using UpNano Think3D software. The models were printed on glass coverslips using UpPhoto resin (UpNano). NanoOne stands out as the most developed printer for mesoscale manufacturing, enabling printing of large structures (10–20 mm in xy and up to 40 mm in height) due to several advanced technologies: a submerged printing mode in a large resin reservoir, high-power 1,000 W, 780-nm laser for fast printing with 5 × 0.25 numerical aperture (NA) objective and adaptive resolution technology that significantly reduces print times (up to 450 mm3 h−1). After printing, the coverslips were washed in isopropanol and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS was cast, degassed, cured at 80 °C and then replicas were cut and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This method allowed us to fabricate high-quality prototypes for validation of the 3D microstructural design elements. However, the main limitation is the upscaling technology for fabrication of the large number of chips. More importantly, process flow is still resulting in the 3D topography features only from one side of the PDMS replica. To overcome the latter problem, commonly some laboratories fabricate multi-layered PDMS chips. In this approach, individual PDMS layers are fabricated separately, aligned and plasma bonded together. This direction was explored early on for fabrication of a few prototypes; however, the alignment process is tedious and unsuitable for large-scale chip manufacturing with the acceptable quality. To address this, inspired by industrial injection molding technology, we developed a cassette mold for PDMS curing. Molds were manufactured by CNC milling of acrylic, aluminum or steel, depending on the desired feature size and quality. Each cassette consisted of two mold parts bearing microtopographies of the bottom and top surfaces of the chip. When assembled, the parts fit precisely, enabling accurate alignment of both sides of the device. PDMS was injected into centre space of the mold, degassed in a vacuum chamber and cured in an 80 °C oven. After curing, the mold was opened and the PDMS sheets were cut and bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This process overcomes many of the limitations of previously described techniques and enables scalable production of hundreds of high-quality chips in a single batch. The main drawback is the need to adapt design features for CNC milling: some of the smallest features must be enlarged and sharp corners rounded. However, we did not consider this as a drawback as concurrently we began exploring industrial plastic molding technologies to eliminate the last remaining problem: the PDMS material itself. Although PDMS is ideal for prototyping, its high absorption of small molecules makes it unsuitable for translational applications and drug testing. Many of the learnings and design optimizations from the PDMS cassette-molding process were directly translated into the design of the final injection-molded plastic chip. Currently, the chip body is fabricated from cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) due to its low shrinkage, chemical resistance and optical transmission. The main body was fabricated as a single piece, followed by bonding of a 170-μm COC film to the bottom surface. A matching lid converting the slide was later designed and produced separately also via a COC injection molding process. After assembly, chips were packaged and sterilized using ethylene oxide gas. Large-scale chip production was outsourced to an external manufacturing facility.

Industry observers note that stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS via replica molding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion (latest version). Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consisted of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 70 to 120 μm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 μm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a 10 × 0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mold with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mold for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

Sources indicate that to generate the ECM for the chip bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized following the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) in 87.5:12.5 (v/v) ratio. A PDMS stamp with crypt-mimmicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir. After the gel injection through the gel-loading port, the hydrogel was polymerized on a 37 °C hotplate for 10 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium. Prepared chips with hydrogels can be stored for multiple weeks at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as ‘incubator’) or in the +4 °C fridge before use. Hydrogel stiffness was measured using an MCR 702e MultiDrive oscillatory shear rheometer (Anton Paar) in a parallel plate configuration with a PP25/P3 measuring plate. The Young’s modulus (E) was estimated from the storage modulus (G′), assuming the hydrogel is elastic and nearly incompressible, using the relation E = 2 G(1 + ν) ≈ 3 G′, where Poisson’s ratio (ν) is approximately 0.5. Across multiple batches and replicates, the hydrogels yielded a Young’s modulus of 3,000 ± 500 Pa.

In brief, intestinal tissue was processed by removal of the underlying muscularis, serosa and fat from the basal side of the intestinal tissue using forceps and scissors. The remaining mucosal tissue was thoroughly washed with DPBS (10010-015, Gibco), supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin (1,500 U ml−1; 15140122, Gibco), gentamicin (500 µg ml−1; 15750060, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and primocin (50 µg ml−1; ant-pm1, Invivogen) before using a glass coverslip to remove excess mucus from the luminal side and blood vessels from the basal side.

To circumvent the poor viability and phenotypic alterations associated with traditional enzymatic disassociations66,67, we adapted and optimized a scaffold-based egression method68 that we have previously shown maximizes tissue-resident immune cell recovery and maintains phenotypic integrity40. As previously reported40, our characterization via scRNA-seq and flow cytometry analysis showed that the vast majority of the isolated cells are TRM cells. Therefore, we used the term TRM cells to describe the total immune cell fraction isolated from intestinal tissue. By flow cytometry, we characterized them as TRM cells based on the assessment of one or multiple of the following markers CD45RO+, CD69+, CD103+, CD45RA− and CCR7−.

Sources indicate that cleaned tissue was cut into square pieces (approximately 5 × 5 mm3) with a scalpel. Next, each fragment was loaded onto a 9 × 9 × 1.5 mm3 tantalum-coated, carbon-based scaffold (MSPP23281-1-REV-A, Ultramet) and cultured in 24-well plates (CC7682-7524, CytoOne) containing 2 ml of cytokine-free immune medium (Supplementary Table 1). Twenty-four hours later, scaffolds with tissue on were removed, and egressed cells were harvested from the bottom of the wells by thorough pipetting. Cells were then counted and biobanked in CryoStor (C2874, Sigma-Aldrich) before further use.

For isolation of donor-matched crypts for organoid establishment, an adjacent clean tissue piece (approximately 3 cm2) was used. Intestinal villi were removed from the tissue by using a glass coverslip. The tissue was then incubated on ice in DPBS + 10 mM EDTA (15575020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a shaker for 30 min. Next, a coverslip was used to scrape off the crypts of the tissue. Crypts were collected in organoid medium (Supplementary Table 1). Crypts were centrifuged and resuspended in GFR Matrigel (356231, Corning). After polymerization for 15 min at 37 °C, organoid medium was added with 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies). Following organoid formation, organoids were passaged every 7 days (up to a maximum of 25 passages). After three passages, organoid mycoplasma tests (LT07-710, Lonza) were performed. All lines used in this study were verified as negative for mycoplasma. Organoid banking was performed using CELLBANKER 1 (11888, Nippon Zenyaku Kogyo). Passaging was performed as previously described52. In brief, organoid medium was removed and wells were washed with DPBS. Next, 500 µl of Gentle Cell Dissociation reagent (07174, Stemcell Technologies) was added and incubated for 2 min at room temperature before collecting the domes in a Falcon tube. After a further 15 min of incubation at room temperature, the suspension was centrifuged at 350g at 4 °C for 5 min. After removal of liquid, the pellet was harshly resuspended with organoid wash medium (Supplementary Table 1) to break the organoids. Broken organoids were centrifuged at 500g and the supernatant discarded before pellet resuspension in GFR Matrigel.

It has been revealed that to generate LGR5, CDH1 and H2BC4 reporter lines, targeting vectors were designed as previously described69. Human intestinal organoids were incubated with 1.25% DMSO (v/v) and 10 µM Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) 24 h before electroporation. Organoids (amounting to approximately 1 million cells per condition) were harvested, dissociated to clumps of 3–5 cells with TrypLE (12604-013, Gibco), washed twice with Optimem (31985070, Gibco) and then resuspended in High Performance Electroporation Solution (45-0805, BTXpress) containing up to 10 µg of targeting vector and 10 µg of Cas9 and guide RNA-expressing vector. Cells were electroporated using the NEPA21 Super Electroporator (Nepagene) with settings as previously described70. Y-27632 was kept for 48 h post-single-cell seeding in growth factor-reduced Matrigel (356231, Corning). Reporter-positive organoids were either picked manually or enriched via FACS.

Recent findings suggest that to generate IL-18 gene knockouts, cells were transfected with 20 µg Cas9–GFP and guide RNA expression constructs at a 1:8 ratio and incubated overnight in culture medium containing 5% Matrigel. Transfected cells were FACS enriched and allowed to grow for 10–14 days. Up to eight clones were manually picked and genotyped by Sanger sequencing of the targeted locus.

Recent findings suggest that S.Tm NCTC 12023 (identical to ATCC14028) and SL1344 WT and isogenic mutant strains were used as listed in Supplementary Table 1. If required for detection of Salmonella by GFP expression, plasmid pFPV25.1 was introduced by electroporation and maintained by selection with 50 µg ml−1 carbenicillin (Roth).

It has been revealed that mutant strains with deletion in invG or steE were generated by λ-Red recombination as previously described71 using pKD13 as template for amplification with Del13 primer sets (synthesized by IDT) listed in Supplementary Table 1, and pWRG730 for expression for λ-Red recombinase functions72. Proper insertion of the aph resistance cassette in target genes was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck for primers and K1 Red-Del. If required, the aph resistance cassette was removed by FLP recombination mediated by helper plasmid pE-FLP73. Resulting clones were checked for loss of kanamycin resistance and pE-FLP, and FLP-mediated deletion was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck For/Rev primer sets.

Strain MvP3487 was generated by P22 transduction of the ΔssaV::aph allele into MvP1764 according to standard procedures. Resulting mutant strains were checked for the absence of lysogens.

It has been revealed that for seeding of the chips—hereafter referred to as ‘engineered intestines’ once intestinal epithelial cells are included—approximately 4-day-old human intestinal organoids from different regions of the gastrointestinal tract (duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon) between passages 5 and 25 were collected in base medium (Supplementary Table 1) and transferred to a 15-ml Falcon tube. Following centrifugation at 300g at 4 °C for 4 min, the base medium was aspirated and the pellet was thoroughly resuspended in base medium. After repeating the centrifugation step, organoids were singularized with TrypLE express solution (12604-013, Gibco) containing 250 U ml−1 DNase I (4536282001, Roche) and 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) for 8 min at 37 °C before harsh resuspension. This step was performed twice before swiftly blocking the dissociation by adding base medium with 10% FBS. Next, cells were passed through a 40-µm strainer (43-50040-51, PluriSelect) before centrifugation at 500g at 4 °C for 4 min. Afterwards, the cells were resuspended in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) containing 10 µm Y-27632. Approximately 1.5 × 105 cells were seeded in a volume of 3 µl onto each micropatterned hydrogel. Approximately 150 µl chip medium with 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestines, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow the cells to attach to the ECM. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl chip medium (+10 µm Y-27632 + 5% FBS) was carefully added to the mid-chamber to avoid cell detachment. Culture medium was exchanged every second day. Approximately 5% of FBS supplementation was removed after the second day (details in Supplementary Table 1).

It has been revealed that on the day of hydrogel seeding, TRM cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells were thawed following our previously described protocol52. T cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells using the EasySep Human T Cell Isolation kit (17951, Stemcell Technologies) and EasySep Magnet (18000, Stemcell Technologies) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Viability and number of immune cells were assessed with Trypan Blue (216040, Invitrogen) on a Countess II (Invitrogen). If the viability of the thawed TRM cells crawl-out was less than 75% (due to remaining tissue debris), Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was applied with MS columns (130-042-201, Miltenyi Biotec) on the OctoMACS separator (130-042-109, Miltenyi Biotec) following the manufacturer’s instructions (typically improved to more than 85% viability). Afterwards, immune cells were placed in the incubator until further processing. Chips were prepared as described above until hydrogel loading. Then, approximately 1 × 105 immune cells were mixed with 6 µl of ECM per chip. Next, 26 µl of ECM was dispensed through the loading port per chip into the mid-reservoir. Immediately after, 6 µl of the ECM-immune suspension was carefully dispensed onto a flipped PDMS stamp, with the micropattern facing upwards, and transferred using forceps onto the previously dispensed ECM in the mid-reservoir of the engineered intestine. Next, immune-hydrogel suspensions were polymerized at 37 °C for 15 min. After polymerization of the ECM, the immune chip slide was topped up with immune chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to ease microstamp removal. After organoid dissociation and epithelial cell seeding as described above, 150 µl immune chip medium containing 500 pg ml−1 IL-15 (570306, BioLegend) and 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestine, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow for cells to attach to the ECM of the engineered intestine. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15 + 10 µm Y-27632) was carefully added to the mid-chamber. Immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15) was exchanged every second day.

Sources indicate that to assess the effects of bacterial components on TRM cells in suspension, LPS (100 ng ml−1; L3024-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and flagellin (50 ng ml−1; tlrl-epstfla-5, InvivoGen) were supplemented in immune medium and cultured for 48 h. Similarly, IL-15 (500 pg ml−1) and IL-18 (10 ng ml−1; 592106, BioLegend) were added in immune medium for TRM cell suspension cultures, either individually or in combination, for 48 h. For the assessment of T cell activation in response to the epithelial secretome, conditioned medium was harvested from the basal reservoirs of epithelium-only chips 48 hpi with S.Tm. This medium was collected, transferred to plates and maintained at −80 °C until the day of the experiment. Upon thawing, condition medium was mixed 1:1 (v/v) with fresh immune medium supplemented with 1,000 pg ml−1 of IL-15, resulting in a final concentration of 500 pg ml−1 of IL-15. TRM cells were subsequently cultured in this mixture for 48 h in suspension. Following these culture periods, cells were subjected to analysis by flow cytometry.

In a recent development, for baseline phenotyping, immune cells were recovered from intestinal resections, filtered through a 40-µm strainer and processed directly. For assessment of luminal content, cells were recovered from the accessible luminal reservoir of the chips. For chip-harvested samples and suspension-cultured TRM cells intended for intracellular cytokine assessment, samples were treated with a protein transport inhibitor cocktail (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h before harvest. To achieve single-cell suspension of tissues for staining, samples were retrieved via a 3-mm biopsy punch and transferred to warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1; 11088858001, Millipore) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1; T9128, Sigma). Samples were incubated in a shaker (1,000 rpm at 37 °C) for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. Following visible disintegration, cells were centrifuged (500g for 3 min), resuspended in Accutase with DNAse I (40 U ml−1) and incubated for 10 min at room temperature until a single-cell suspension was achieved. All samples were filtered (40 µm) and washed twice in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS) before staining.

Cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) in Brilliant Stain Buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) for 10 min at room temperature in PBS, followed by a fixable viability dye in PBS (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher) for 10 min following centrifugation. Surface antibodies were applied in FACS buffer for 15 min at room temperature. Following centrifugation and surface labelling, samples were processed according to their experimental requirement. Baseline samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 min at room temperature. Intracellular cytokine samples were fixed using IC fixation buffer (30 min in the dark at room temperature; 15284728, Invitrogen), washed in 1X permeabilization buffer (15284728, Invitrogen) and incubated with intracellular antibodies for 30 min at room temperature. Finally, samples were washed once more in 1X permeabilization buffer before centrifugation.

In a recent development, cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) and brilliant stain buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) in FACS buffer for 15 min at 4 °C. Without washing, a 2X concentrated antibody master mix of chemokine receptors (CX3CR1, CXCR5, CCR7 and CD103) was added directly and incubated for 20 min at 37 °C in the incubator. Following centrifugation, the remaining surface antibodies and streptavidin were applied in FACS buffer for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by a single wash with PBS and centrifugation. Viability dye was then added in PBS for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by centrifugation. To fix and permeabilize the cells for intracellular cytokine and transcription factor staining, the FoxP3 kit (00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions (30 min at 4 °C).
