Recent findings suggest that the relationship between angiosperm and bee richness probably reflects a combination of shared biogeographic drivers, such as area and climate, as well as ecological dependence, although the contribution of these factors cannot be separated here. However, the markedly higher baseline bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands at equivalent angiosperm richness is consistent with the hypothesis that temperature seasonality promotes bee specialization57. Seasonal climates can promote bee specialization through temporal resource partitioning while perhumid tropical systems, despite higher plant richness, may present ecological filters that limit bee diversity. Therefore, capturing more detailed information on the complex networks that wild bees form with native plants, and how they vary with island isolation and reduced colonization events, is crucial for developing more complete models of island biodiversity58,59 (reviewed in ref. 1). Yet recent evidence highlights that flowering plant communities may be reliant on bee pollinators when bee richness is comparatively low60. Consequently, we should not expect a simple, predictable relationship between plant and bee richness across islands of differing biomes, isolation and area.

Our study demonstrates that islands account for a substantial share of global bee diversity, including many species that evolved on islands and are endemic. We find that species richness and endemism are partly disconnected, highlighting that these two metrics capture distinct aspects of insular bee diversity. Richness peaks in mid-latitude, Mediterranean-type islands in the Northern Hemisphere, whereas peak endemism occurs in large tropical islands, with these differences being strongest for oceanic islands. These patterns are further supported by the biome-dependent relationship between angiosperm and bee richness, showing that although floral richness is a strong predictor of bee diversity across islands, it does not fully account for the differences in bee richness observed among biomes. Only a small percentage of island bee species have been assessed for extinction risk29,30, and this risk is probably tied to evolutionary distinctiveness rather than richness55. Therefore, our results suggest that conserving bees on islands requires prioritization of areas of unique evolutionary history, from large continental fragments such as Madagascar to remote oceanic archipelagos like the Hawaiian islands, over species richness alone.

Recent findings suggest that bees are particularly well suited as a model taxon for studying island biogeographical dynamics. They are pivotal pollinators that are closely linked to plant reproduction and ecosystem functioning22, and represent a taxonomically discrete group with an increasing availability of distributional and phylogenetic data. However, much remains to be explored in understanding the mechanisms behind the patterns of colonization and speciation, and the potential for upcoming discoveries. The increasing availability of molecular phylogenies opens up new research avenues for addressing the evolutionary history of bees27. Combined with detailed distribution and trait data61, these resources make it possible to reconstruct historical patterns of colonization, extinction and speciation on islands. With the baseline established here, we lay the foundation for understanding the colonization, diversification and vulnerability of insect diversity on islands more broadly.

Industry observers note that we verified the presence of bees on islands on the basis of information available on Discover Life (https://www.discoverlife.org/) and more detailed and recently updated information, notably, for type locality and collection event data, extracted from source files for that resource21. These expert-vetted lists were filtered for island records and joined with spatial data to align species presence with island identifiers. The checklist data on Discover Life were collected from a variety of sources, including taxonomic revisions, primary species descriptions (including synonyms), verified human observations, and undigitized museum records. To avoid complications from historical boundary changes, species were recorded at the current state or country level. The data are available online as a matrix at the country level, with species-specific details provided for finer geographic scales. For further details on how the checklists were sourced see ref. 4. For islands not clearly associated with a specific country or state/province, additional sources were used to confirm species presence based on the broader political region. We then cross-referenced specimens with island-specific faunal checklists from the published literature; for example, when a species was known only from an archipelago we tried to determine its presence on specific islands within the archipelago. These included studies from Abd al Kuri and Socotra from the Socotra Archipelago65, the Azores including Corvo, Faial, Flores, Graciosa, Pico, Santa Maria, São Jorge, São Miguel and Terceira66, Balearic Islands including Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca67, Bonaire68, Cabo Verde including Boa Vista, Brava, Sal, Santiago, Santo Antão, São Nicolau and São Vicente69, Cuba and East Grand Bahama70, Fiji52,71, Isla de Juventud72, Juan Fernández Islands73, Madeira Archipelago including Madeira, Porto Santo, and Deserto Grande and Selvagens Islands including Selvagem Grande74 and Madagascar75,76. European island checklists were extracted from the latest checklists for European species from Reverte et al.77 and included Åland islands, Great Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Faroe Islands, Malta, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, Crete, Cyprus and Isle of Man. We also included validated (Research Grade) iNaturalist records (up to December 2024) for all islands available from the initial checklists. Although these entries provide valuable data, a degree of taxonomic doubt remains, consequently, they have been labelled as uncertain within the final dataset pending further validation. The checklists for the Greek islands of Corfu and Rhodes were expanded with records from Rhodes78,79, Corfu80 and the personal collection of T. J. Wood. Recent additions to Corsica and Sardinia were also added81, as were the latest checklists of the Canary Islands82. Finally, the bee fauna of Tasmania was significantly adjusted due to recent taxonomic work on the Parasphecodes subgenus83. Names were cleaned using the synonym lists from Orr et al.4 and Dorey et al.84. In some cases, it was not possible to separate archipelago-level data into island records and some archipelagos were therefore retained in the dataset (for example, for the Solomon Islands).

To classify non-native species and calculate final island native species richness, we used Russo85 as a baseline, complemented by existing checklist information and expert opinion from J.S.A. Using the checklists, we calculated three measures of wild bee richness and endemism on islands. They included: (1) native species richness, calculated as the total number of unique native species included in the checklist for each island (or archipelago, as the case may be); (2) single-island endemism, calculated as the total number of species on the checklist only known from that island; (3) AE, calculated as the total number of species found only on that archipelago: this includes all SIEs.

In a recent development, using the above checklists, we extracted a spatially explicit database of islands by matching the names from the checklist to those found in the global islands (greater than 1 km2 in area) database of Sayre et al.63. We extracted a vector shapefile of all islands for which we had any wild bee checklist information. In most cases we endeavoured to associate each checklist with a single island entity. In cases where a single name from the bee database is associated with multiple land masses, we extracted all the landmasses for subsequent calculations (for example, Sao Tome and Principe, Saint Vincent and Grenadines, Wallis and Futuna, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Pierre and Miquelon, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Solomon Islands). Duplicate island names and spatial mismatches were checked manually. Following this we harmonized the island names with the islands included in the Global Inventory of Floras and Traits (GIFT) database and extracted information on island area, isolation (distance to mainland), island category (oceanic, fragment or continental), archipelago and richness of angiosperms from GIFT (for more detail, see ref. 20). Islands in the GIFT database were categorized by geological origin into oceanic (volcanic islands and atolls), continental shelf (land-bridge), and complex origin/continental fragments. Categorizing islands into three discrete types is a necessary simplification. Certain cases, such as the tectonic uplift of Cyprus or continental fragments such as Rhodes, Fresh Caledonia and Seram that underwent periods of total submergence, represent intermediate states where biological isolation was prioritized over strict geological origin. Specifically, a lack of historical land-bridge connections was used to classify islands as oceanic in type. Of the final 305 islands, there were 207 oceanic islands, 25 fragment islands and 73 continental islands (see Supplementary Table 12 for a full breakdown by biome).

Species distribution data for 350,707 vascular plant species across 1,967 islands and 1,010 mainland regions were taken from Schrader et al.9 and then associated with islands for which we have bee species checklists. These data were originally sourced from the GIFT v.3.2 database using the R package GIFT86 and are taxonomically standardized according to the World Checklist of Vascular Plants9,20. In the few cases where we had bee checklist data for an island or archipelago that did not correspond to an island or archipelago in the GIFT database—for example, data aggregated at archipelago level in one but not the other—we calculated area and isolation directly from the aforementioned spatial map of islands63 and island-specific literature was used to determine island category and archipelago.

We incorporated additional island-level environmental information by overlaying our island shapefile with a spatial global shapefile of ecoregions62, which is an update of the original WWF biogeographical regionalization of Olson et al.87. This dataset provides a globally standardized classification of terrestrial ecoregions, biomes and biogeographic realms, and was selected because it offers consistent, GIS-based borders that explicitly include oceanic islands, allowing reproducible assignment of islands based solely on spatial overlap. Although developed as a general terrestrial biodiversity classification rather than for specific taxa, the underlying climatic, floristic and evolutionary discontinuities that define these realms are expected to also be relevant for bees, whose distributions are closely tied to vegetation structure and climatic regimes. Each island was assigned to a terrestrial biome and biogeographic realm using the intersect function from the R package sf (v1.0-2188). Biome classifications were aggregated into broader categories (boreal, desert, Mediterranean, temperate and tropical) for comparative purposes (Supplementary Table 13) and the final selected biome was the dominant biome found on the island. Realm classifications were one of Afrotropic, Australasia, Indomalaya, Nearctic, Neotropic, Oceania and Palaearctic. This allowed for consistent ecological context across islands and facilitated analyses of native bee richness by biome type and realm.

Industry observers note that we also calculated additional isolation metrics by computing the edge-to-edge distance (km) from each study island to the nearest landmass across three size classes (>1 km2, >1,000 km2 and >10,000 km2) and the cumulative surrounding land area (km2) within buffers of 10 km, 100 km and 1,000 km around each island. To do this, we combined our global island database with a global continental layer from rnaturalearth v1.0.189. We tested correlations (r > 0.7) among all isolation variables prior to model fitting (Supplementary Fig. 1). We selected distance to the nearest landmass >1,000 km2 and the total land area within the 10 km buffer to represent isolation, alongside distance to mainland (km), in the final set of variables with which we conducted model selection. Climate data were extracted from bioclimatic rasters from the CHELSA v2.190 with a resolution of 30 arcsec. The variables included annual mean temperature (BIO1), temperature seasonality (BIO4; defined as the standard deviation of monthly mean temperatures multiplied by 100), annual precipitation (BIO12), and precipitation seasonality (BIO15; defined as the coefficient of variation of monthly precipitation). Local elevation metrics were extracted for each island using the elevatr package (v0.99.1)91. Climate variables were averaged for each island and elevation was recorded as the elevational range of each island.

To ensure comparability and ecological and biogeographical relevance, we limited our final dataset to islands with a minimum area of 5 km2 and located at least 1 km from the mainland. These thresholds helped to remove islands with high edge effects, and limited habitat heterogeneity, while ensuring a meaningful biogeographical break from the mainland.

To explore global patterns of bee sampling on islands we used the BeeBDC protocol outlined in Dorey et al.84 to extract all global records of bees on islands. Specifically, we downloaded all records of Anthophila from Global Biodiversity Information Facility92, Atlas of Living Australia93 and iDigBio. We corrected synonymous names as above using the synonym lists from Dorey et al.84 and Orr et al.4. As part of the cleaning process the data were subset to only include names of species found in the island checklist dataset, ensuring incorrect records of valid species unlikely to occur on the island were removed. To link bee occurrence records with islands spatially, we reprojected all coordinates to match the island shapefile and performed a spatial join, retaining only records intersecting island polygons defined in the checklist dataset. To ensure consistency between occurrence and checklist data, all species listed in the island checklists were added as supplementary records to the public database, standardizing species richness values across sources. The final dataset comprised 663,189 georeferenced records, which were subsequently used to assess sampling effort and spatial coverage across islands included in the analysis. This dataset was used to calculate a proxy for sampling effort and sampling completeness. To measure sampling completeness we calculated sampling coverage across islands using the Chao & Jost64 method via the coverage function in the iNEXT3D R package (v1.08)94. We used a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). To account for large differences in sampling effort we additionally weighted coverage based on the total number of occurrence records, subsequently referred to as a sample-size-adjusted measure of sampling completeness.

We used the Discover Life global checklist through the BeeBDC tool84 as our baseline source for global bee species richness. To generate an estimate of mainland-only species richness, we excluded all species known to occur on islands by comparing with the above checklists and by removing all island-level records from the global checklist. The global checklist was also used to supplement endemism and island-only species data by filtering out species only recorded on islands from the checklist and cross-referencing with the island dataset. The mainland checklist was also used to test island occurrence patterns to create a binary classification of all species as either occurring or not occurring on islands.

We used the island-level checklists to test the key predictors of species richness on islands. We fit a linear mixed-effects model using the lmer function from the lme4 R package (v1.1-37)95, with native species richness as the response variable. We log10-transformed native species richness after adding 1 to all values to accommodate islands with zero native bee species (n = 4) while preserving them in the analysis.

In a recent development, we constructed a full model including the full set of ecological predictors, and then tested all possible model subsets (dredge function, R package MuMIn v1.48.1196). In all models, log10-transformed island area and a measure of island isolation were retained as fixed effects because these variables represent the core predictions of island biogeography theory. We evaluated three alternative isolation metrics in separate full models: log10-transformed distance to the nearest mainland, log10-transformed distance to the nearest landmass exceeding 1,000 km2, and the surrounding land area in a 10 km buffer around the island.

The full model also included biome (5 categories), elevation range (log10), mean annual temperature (scaled), temperature seasonality (log10), annual precipitation (log10), precipitation seasonality (log10), island type (continental, fragment, or oceanic), and sampling completeness (sample-size-adjusted coverage, log10). We also evaluated an Area × Biome interaction and an Isolation × Biome interaction. We assessed collinearity among predictors using variance inflation factors (VIF; R package car, vif function97); mean annual temperature showed high collinearity with biome and other climate variables across all datasets (VIF > 5), and removing it from the full model brought all remaining predictors below this threshold. We therefore excluded mean annual temperature from the full model. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept in all models to account for spatial non-independence among islands within the same archipelago and to allow baseline species richness to vary among archipelagos98. Models were fit by maximum likelihood and ranked by AICc; models with all three isolation-metric were then pooled into a single ranked set of models. When more than one model was within ΔAICc < 2, we selected the simplest model with the fewest degrees of freedom (Supplementary Table 4). The best-supported model included:.

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Isolation)ij + β5 × IslandTypeij + β6 × SamplingCompletenessij + uj + εij.

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = number of native bee species observed on island i in archipelago j.

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km).

IslandTypeij = island type (continental, fragment, oceanic).

SamplingCompletenessij = sample-size-adjusted coverage.

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome.

β4 = effect of log10(isolation)β5 = effects of island type.

β6 = effect of sampling completeness.

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

The final model included the interaction between area and biome, indicating that the effect of area on species richness varies among biomes. Island type and sampling completeness were retained as fixed effects. Two island groups for which coverage could not be calculated were dropped from the final model (Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn Islands, n = 303). We quantified variance explained by fixed effects alone using marginal R2 and using conditional R2 for variance explained by both fixed and random effects99. To compare species–area relationship slopes among biomes, we extracted biome-specific slopes and their standard errors from the variance–covariance matrix of fixed effects. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (v1.11.1)101. Model predictions and confidence intervals were generated using the fixed-effects design matrix and visualized using ggplot2 (v3.5.2)102. Finally, we fit the same best model for only oceanic and only continental and fragment islands, specifically to compare ISAR slopes among biomes of different island types.

Recent findings suggest that to explore the predictors of endemic species richness and its relationship with total species richness across islands, we used a model selection approach mirroring our richness analysis. We fit a series of linear mixed-effects models using the lmer function from the R package lme4 (v1.1-37)95. Collinearity among predictors was assessed the same way as for richness and mean annual temperature was also removed from all endemism full models.

We focused on islands supporting at least one single-island endemic (SIE ≥ 1; n = 113 islands). In this subset of islands, all biomes are represented apart from boreal, as the boreal islands harboured no endemics. We used the same model fitting procedure as described for the native richness analysis. All models within ΔAICc < 2 are shown in Supplementary Table 7. The best-supported model included:.

log10(Endemism)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(TemperatureSeasonality)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij.

Endemismij = number of single-island endemic bee species observed on island i in archipelago j.

TemperatureSeasonalityij = temperature seasonality.

Isolationij = distance to nearest landmass >1,000 km2.

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome.

β4 = effect of log10(temperature seasonality).

β5 = effect of log10(isolation).

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

To assess the generality of endemism patterns, we repeated analyses on three subsets: (1) oceanic islands only (n = 69), where endemism is more probably driven by neo-endemic evolution rather than the retention of land-bridge palaeo-endemics; (2) endemic-rich islands (SIE > 5% of total richness; n = 96), focusing on systems where endemism is well-established. We also repeated all analyses for AEs (species endemic to entire archipelagos; AE ≥ 1; n = 217) to confirm patterns were robust across endemism definitions (Supplementary Tables 5 and  7). The archipelago-level approach captures archipelago-wide diversification processes while revealing which individual islands within archipelagos are endemism hotspots (see, for example, ref. 48). For the SIE ≥ 1 and oceanic island subsets, the variance of the archipelago random effect was estimated at zero; however, it was kept for consistency across all models.

Additionally, to formally test how the relationship between richness and endemism varies across biomes, we compared three nested models for SIEs and AEs:.

where endemism is predicted solely by richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + (1|Archipelago);.

where biome adds information beyond richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + Biome + (1|Archipelago); and.

where the slope of the effect of richness varies by biome: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) × Biome + (1|Archipelago).

We compared these nested models sequentially using likelihood ratio tests. If including biome as a fixed effect significantly improves model fit, this indicates that islands with similar richness support different baseline levels of endemism depending on biome. If including the interaction between biome and richness improves model fit then the rate at which endemics accumulate with increasing richness also varies across biomes. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101.

To assess the extent to which bee diversity tracks angiosperm diversity across islands, we fitted a linear regression model with native bee richness as the response variable and native angiosperm richness and its interaction with biome as the predictors. We additionally included both island area and isolation as covariates to account for confounding geographic effects that influence the richness of both angiosperms and bees. Variance inflation factors indicated low multicollinearity among predictors (all VIFs < 2.4), supporting the inclusion of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation in the same model. We fit the model for the 175 islands for which we had both bee native richness data and reliable angiosperm richness data from the GIFT database20. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept to account for spatial non-independence of islands within the same archipelago. To include the interaction with biome we removed boreal islands from the analysis as there were too few islands (3) with which to test the interaction.

Industry observers note that to (1) compare baseline shifts (intercepts) across biomes against a single baseline and (2) to conduct a likelihood ratio test on the significance of the interaction between biome and angiosperm richness, we additionally fitted a model with and without the angiosperm richness × biome interaction term. The full model with interaction was:.

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(AngiospermRichness)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(AngiospermRichness)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Area)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij.

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = native bee species richness on island i in archipealgo j.

AngiospermRichnessij = native angiosperm species richness.

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km).

β1 = effect of log10(angiosperm richness).

β3 = interaction between log10(angiosperm richness) and biome.

β5 = effect of log10(isolation).

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

It has been revealed that using the coefficients from this model, we computed an adjusted bee richness for each island by subtracting the centred contributions of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation from the observed values. This adjustment standardizes the data, showing the bee richness for each island if it had the global average plant richness, land area, and isolation. Finally, we calculated estimated marginal means for each biome using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101, and performed post hoc pairwise comparisons (FDR correction)100.

Recent findings suggest that all statistical analyses, data manipulation, and visualizations were conducted in R (v4.5.0)103. In addition to the packages already cited; data processing, post hoc tests, and figure formatting were carried out using the following packages: broom.mixed (v0.2.9.6)104, ComplexUpset (v1.3.3)105, corrplot (v0.95)106, cowplot (v1.2.0)107, ggnewscale (v0.5.1)108, ggrepel (v0.9.6)109, ggtext (v0.1.2)110, kableExtra (v1.4.0)111, lmerTest (v3.1-3)112, maps (v3.4.2.1)113, mgcv (v1.9-4)114, multcomp (v1.4-28)115, multcompView (v0.1−10)116, patchwork (v1.3.0)117, performance (v0.13.0)118, scales (v1.4.0)119, scico (v1.5.0)120, tidyverse (v2.0.0)121 and UpSetR (v1.4.1)122.

(A) Biome-specific island species–area relationships. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.15, 95% CI = [−0.26, −0.03], t(130.5) = −2.56, p = 0.012). Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Sources indicate that (A) Biome-specific island species–area relationships. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.05, 95% CI = [−0.18, 0.08], t(75.7) = 0.72, p = 0.475). Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Sampling completeness is represented by the log10-transformed sample-size-adjusted coverage on each island. The effect of sampling completeness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.22, 95% CI = [0.13,0.31], t(294.5) = 4.73, p = 3.46 × 10−6). n = 303 islands.

Recent findings suggest that (A) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and single-island endemic (SIE) species richness for oceanic islands with at least one single-island endemic (n = 69 islands). Solid black line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of area was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.32, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.42], t(69) = 6.23, p = 3.18 × 10−8). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic. (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to nearest mainland, km) and SIE richness for oceanic islands. Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.05, 95% CI = [−0.17, 0.06], t(69) = −0.92, p = 0.36). (C) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and single-island endemic (SIE) species richness for islands where endemics comprise more than 5% of native bee richness (n = 96 islands). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of area was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.36, 95% CI = [0.30, 0.43], t(69.8) = 10.74, p = 2 × 10−16). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic. (D) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to nearest mainland, km) and SIE richness for endemic-rich islands. Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.07, 95% CI = [−0.20, 0.06], t(75.8) = −1.06, p = 0.29). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic.

Industry observers note that (A) Single-island endemics (n = 113 islands). (B) Archipelago endemics species that are archipelago endemics across biomes (n = 217 islands). Violins show the kernel density distribution of the data. Overlaid box plots represent the median (center line) and 25th and 75th percentiles (bounds of box /interquartile range (IQR)); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5×IQR.

(A) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and archipelago endemic (AE) species richness, for islands with at least one archipelago endemic. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic at the archipelago level. Labelled islands are the top 10% highest in AE richness with the number of AEs in parentheses. (B) Relationship between isolation (log10 km from mainland) and AE richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.04, 95% CI = [−0.17,], t(173) = −0.71, p = 0.48). Circle colour as in panel A. (C) Relationship between elevation range (log10 m) and AE richness. The effect of elevation range was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.18, 95% CI = [0.04, 0.33], t(216.6) = 2.51, p = 0.01). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel B. (D) Relationship between sampling completeness (log10 sample-size-adjusted coverage) and AE richness. The effect of sampling completeness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.24], t(216.8) = 2.50, p = 0.01). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel B.

(A) Relationship between total native species richness (log10) and single-island endemic (SIE) richness (log10), coloured by biome. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Islands with ≥1 SIE (n = 113 islands). (B) Residuals from a linear mixed-effects model of log10(SIE) ~ log10(native richness), with archipelago as a random effect (n = 113 islands)., shown by biome. Values above zero indicate more SIEs than predicted by richness alone; values below zero indicate fewer. Numbers show the median fold-change relative to model predictions. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test; χ² = 33.18, df = 3, p = 2.95 × 10−7) Table S7); letters denote groups that differ significantly based on two-sided post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means (FDR correction, p < 0.05). Overlaid box plots represent the median (center line) and 25th and 75th percentiles (bounds of box/interquartile range (IQR)); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5×IQR. (C) Relationship between total native species richness (log10) and archipelago endemics (AE; islands with at least one AE, n = 217 islands) richness (log10), coloured by biome. Unlike SIE, the rate at which AE accumulates with richness varied significantly among biomes (likelihood ratio test on the richness × biome interaction; χ2 = 32.25, df = 3, p = 4.63 × 10−7; Table S7). Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. (D) Residuals from the AE richness model across biomes (n = 217). Boxplots, violins and letters are the same as in Panel B. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test, χ2 = 40.37, df = 3, p = 8.90 × 10−9; Table S7).

Supplementary Tables 1–6 and 8–13 and Supplementary Fig. 1.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gerry Cardinale had a meeting with the AC Milan management at Casa Milan yesterday, during which there were four key topics, according to reports.

According to recent reports, cardinale has arrived in the city in good time for Milan’s game against Frosinone tomorrow. Yesterday, there was a summit with the Milan management, including the CEO Massimo Calvelli, Head of Football Intelligence Bobby Gardiner, and Head of Recruitment Tiago Estevão.

This was reported by Sky Italia (via MilanEye) and various outlets, highlighting how Cardinale wants to be ready for the January window and even the summer window. Markus Krösche will be there to help him with that, set to be unveiled next week, as Gazzetta dello Sport reported.

According to Daniele Longo, there were four key topics during the meeting: the renewal of Adrien Rabiot (which is close), the Endrick pursuit (which is heating up), Goncalo Inacio for the defence, and Krösche’s announcement.

Industry observers note that there could be a lot of substantial movement in the coming months, in other words, as Cardinale is really pushing for these things to materialise. Of course, other matters were also discussed during the meeting but as Longo highlighted, those mentioned above were the main ones.

Cardinale will be at Milanello today and then he will also be in the stands for the game tomorrow, showing his support for the team yet again.

#72359. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli not feeling the heat after dismal Nations League campaign

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli not feeling the heat after dismal Nations League campaign

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:30 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:40 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Sebastien Pocognoli insists he’s unconcerned about calls for his head after a dismal start to his time in charge of Scotland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:40 EST, 17 November 2026.

Sebastien Pocognoli insists he’s unconcerned about calls for his head after a dismal start to his time in charge of Scotland.

Monday’s 4-0 defeat to Switzerland confirmed that the Belgian’s side finished a distant third in their Nations League section with the only two wins in six games coming against North Macedonia.

After a decent start to the match in St Gallen, Scotland fell behind to a Lewis Ferguson own goal and the result was put beyond doubt when the Swiss scored two quick goals at the outset of the second half.

With another performance falling way short of expectations and little sign of progress, the upcoming manager is increasingly coming under pressure.

Despite only being in charge for 13 weeks, pundits including Michael Stewart have already called on the Scottish Football Association to draw a line under Pocognoli’s reign.

According to recent reports, adamant that he’s not feeling the heat, though, the 39-year-old insisted: ‘I am not thinking about this. I am just looking ahead to the next camp in March and the start of the qualification.

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli is confident he'll get Scotland back on track.

Skipper Andy Robertson reacts at full-time to the 4-0 defeat against Switzerland.

It has been revealed that ‘We have to take the most we can from the last two camps and try to build something strong for the next one. The objective is to reach the Euros in the best position possible.

‘We will have ups and downs and it was not good in terms of the score against Switzerland. But, for me as a coach, it was a good game to see us against a strong nation away from home. That’s something we have to take into the future.’.

Asked how he dealt with the growing clamour for his dismissal, he replied: ‘I don’t accept this to be honest. It’s always like this when you have a bad moment, when you think about the past. But always thinking about the past is an energy taker — we have to look forward.’.

The successor to Steve Clarke, Pocognoli has tried to bring in a more attacking philosophy via a 3-4-2-1 formation.

While his reluctance to adapt has also drawn widespread criticism, he claims he’s not averse to coming up with a different approach.

Industry observers note that ‘It’s possible,’ he added. ‘I did it in Monaco and we won many tough games with a back four. I also won many good games with a back three.

Sources indicate that ‘We played in the Champions League and in half of the games we played with a different shape, so it doesn’t mean that I’m not flexible. But the timeline is to do what we are trying to do now.’.

Industry observers note that asked if the job was proving to be tougher than he anticipated, Pocognoli noted: ‘No. I think we nearly had a good game. It was just the score and the aspects in the boxes. That’s where there’s disappointment.

‘It’s step by step. And we have created a lot of chances in four of the six games. And in these six games we played one of them with 10 men and another where we were not on the level at all against Slovenia.’.

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 13:45, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 13:48.

Bayern Munich and England star Harry Kane has vowed to return for the "business end of the season" after undergoing ankle surgery.

The striker sustained an ankle ligament injury in Bayern's 1-1 draw against FC Koln on Friday evening.

Kane attempted to carry on after being caught in a tackle from Koln defender Joel Schmied before he received treatment and made way for Tom Bischof in the 20th minute.

Bayern released a statement after the game, revealing Kane would be out for a "few months" with a "torn syndesmotic ligament in his left ankle".

Industry observers note that in a fresh upgrade on Saturday morning, Bayern said: "Harry Kane underwent successful surgery overnight following the syndesmosis ligament tear in his left ankle, which he sustained in yesterday’s Bundesliga match against 1. FC Köln.

"The 33-year-old will now begin his rehabilitation program.".

Kane also shared a defiant message on social media, accompanied by an image of him sitting on a hospital bed with his left foot in a protective boot.

"The highs and lows of life!" Kane wrote. "Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it’s an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027.

"I’ll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season!

“‘Tough times don’t last, tough people do’ - my guy Julian Edelman (three-time Super Bowl winner) told me this one!

In a recent development, “Thank you for all the messages! Alles gut!”.

I’ll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season! “Tough times don’t last, tough people do” - my guy @Edelman11 told me this one! Thank you for all the messages! Alles gut! ❤️?

With Kane likely to be out until the end of February, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany will have to come up with solutions to negate the impact of being without his star striker.

Ismael Saibari can play as a centre-forward, but he is currently sidelined with the same injury as Kane, putting him out of action until the start of February.

Serge Gnabry is also on the sidelines and is unlikely to be back until the turn of the year, leaving Kompany without another potential candidate to fill the void created by Kane's absence.

Noah Codjo-Evora is an option if Kompany decides to put his faith in youth, but the 19-year-old is unlikely to start regularly given the fact he only made his first-team debut as a substitute on Friday.

That means Kompany will likely opt to field a false nine in the coming weeks and months, which is a role Lennart Karl played when Kane went off against Koln.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Blues winger had in fact scored in the game, netting his side's second goal at the Cardiff City Stadium, but saw his game fall apart in the second-half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 17:34 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:49 EST, 17 November 2026.

Chelsea star Pedro Neto lost his cool while playing for Portugal in their win over Wales as he received two yellow cards in as many minutes before clashing with opposing manager Craig Bellamy.

The Blues winger had in fact scored in the game, netting his side's second goal at the Cardiff City Stadium, but saw his game fall apart in the second-half.

He was first booked for a high challenge on the back of Brennan Johnson's leg – a tackle which some may argue could have been a red in itself.

One minute and 59 seconds later, he was shown his second yellow when he slid in on Johnson again. He didn't appear to make too much contact, if any, but left the Wales man sprawling to avoid it.

German referee Sven Jablonski showed no hesitation in sending Neto off, but the winger wasn't going to take it lying down.

He had to be held back by captain Bruno Fernandes as he tried to confront Johnson, and seemingly managed to shout in his direction before reluctantly making his way off the field.

Pedro Neto was sent off while playing for Portugal against Wales after two yellow cards in under two minutes.

He also had a confrontation with Wales manager Craig Bellamy (right) as he left the field of play.

Before that, though, he had a conversation with Wales boss Craig Bellamy, with officials initially trying to separate the two, with Neto looking angry.

Bellamy, though, spoke to Neto and embraced him before finally walking down the tunnel.

The 26-year-old will now serve a one-game suspension, meaning he will miss the first leg of Portugal's Nations League quarter-final, which will be played in March.

Jorge Jesus's side secured top spot in their group with the win over Wales, which was achieved by Carlos Forbs's 70th-minute goal.

Fernandes had opened the scoring for his side in the 11th minute, but David Brooks and Sorba Thomas gave Wales an unlikely lead.

That was until Neto levelled things up just before half-time, and Forbs scored the winner, with ten-man Portugal able to hold on for all three points.

Wales finished bottom of the group with one win – against Norway – and five defeats from their six matches.

Captain Ben Davies mentioned after the game: 'We highlighted a lot of character and we've shown good effort in these games where we've just come up short from a results perspective.

After expressing his frustration, the Chelsea star had to be directed off the field by captain Bruno Fernandes (right).

He had in fact scored for his side in the game, bringing them level before the half-time interval.

'There is a lot to take from this going into the games in March and we have to feel confident because we've been playing well.

According to recent reports, 'We know the boys up top can be so dangerous, and if teams want to come here and play man-for-man against us, we've got a lot of speed and we have to be good on the ball. That comes with risk sometimes, like you saw with the chances that they had, but I'd rather play this way and go toe-to-toe with these teams and have a go.

Recent findings suggest that 'We competed in the campaign and we were not a million miles off like the table might suggest. I thought we put in some very good performances, we just wished we had some better results.'.

Neto, meanwhile, will now return to his club side Chelsea ahead of a busy Christmas period.

He has started all but one Premier League game so far and has been a key player under newly introduced manager Xabi Alonso.

The Blues will take on Leeds at Stamford Bridge this weekend as club football returns.

  • Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has recalled goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez for Saturday's Premier League fixture against Leeds United.
  • Despite Martinez having proven his recovery from a fractured jaw for Argentina over the international break, many felt that Mike Penders would retain his place between the sticks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 21 Nov 2026 13:47, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 13:58.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has recalled goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez for Saturday's Premier League fixture against Leeds United.

Despite Martinez having proven his recovery from a fractured jaw for Argentina over the international break, many felt that Mike Penders would retain his place between the sticks.

Instead, Alonso has opted to hand Martinez a way back into the starting lineup in what is one of four changes from the 1-0 defeat at Sunderland.

Josh Acheampong has shaken off a minor fitness issue to take the spot of Marco Palestra at right-back.

Estevao Willian returns on the right flank, with Jordan Henderson dropping down to the substitutes' bench.

Meanwhile, Alonso has selected a frontline number nine, with Emanuel Emegha getting the nod over Pedro Neto for what is his first Premier League start.

Moises Caicedo has passed a fitness test to take his place in midfield.

As for Leeds, Daniel Farke has made just the one alteration to his Leeds XI for the game in West London.

Noah Okafor has been rewarded for his goal as a substitute versus Spurs with a place in the final third ahead of Lukas Nmecha.

Sean Longstaff will either line up in a three-player midfield or be used as one of two number 10s.

Chelsea XI: Martinez; Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria; Lavia, Caicedo; Estevao, Palmer, Rogers; Emegha.

Subs: Penders, Subuloye, Gusto, Palestra, Barco, Henderson, Neto, Quenda, Welbeck.

Leeds United XI: Trafford; Bogle, Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic, Gudmundsson; Ampadu, Longstaff, Tanaka; Okafor, Calvert-Lewin.

Subs: Zetterer, Bard, Rodon, Bijol, Stach, Aaronson, James, Wilson, Nmecha.

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he rolled out a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

Sources indicate that they certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Industry observers note that ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a significant game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC.

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

Industry observers note that on the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30.

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Recent findings suggest that martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring problems to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the organization man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

It has been revealed that that Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

According to recent reports, good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

According to recent reports, atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

It has been revealed that simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

It has been revealed that the one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#72331. 'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.
  • Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026.

In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.

Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game. The club are already on a run of five defeats in seven.

Moments like this reveal the Blackpool fanbase’s deep sense of perspective, born of their long and often wretched fight to kick out one of British football’s most detested owners, Owen Oyston.

‘We’re still here and we’re watching our club home and away,’ says Andy Higgins, chair of the Blackpool Supporters Trust. ‘We have a good relationship with the club,’ says his friend Dave Ragozzino, with Higgins in the Earlsfield pub. ‘The club are asking us to tell fans what’s going on, and they know we will help. Ten years ago, our club’s owners were suing us.’.

The story of the campaign which brought these fans and many more together is told in a superb new documentary The Battle for Blackpool, which screens this week, capturing its spirit, imagination and intelligence.

Oyston and his son Karl have both cooperated with the documentary-makers. Oyston Snr, wearing dark shades and his trademark fedora, is interviewed at his stately home in the Forest of Bowland, while his son Karl, clearly still consumed with hate and contempt for fans, is filmed clay pigeon shooting across their estate.

Blackpool fans watch their team fall to another League One defeat, at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday.

The Tangerines are just two points above the relegation zone having lost five out of their last seven league fixtures.

Their supporters fought a long and wretched battle against the club's former owner Owen Oyston (pictured in 2017).

The film’s stars are the supporters who led the fight – Christine Seddon, Tim Fielding, Ragozzino, two fans in a Mk1 tangerine Golf GTI and twin sisters of advancing years who embraced the campaign’s guerilla tactics.

Recent findings suggest that oyston Jr, who chaired the club at his mother’s request after his father was jailed for rape in 1996, tells the documentary-makers: ‘My father likes football. I didn’t.’.

It was after he’d stumbled on a managerial genius in Ian Holloway, who took the club into the Premier League for a season in 2010-11, that a full sense of the family’s greed and entitlement became clear.

According to recent reports, the Mail on Sunday's Nick Harris revealed that Oyston Snr had paid himself £11million out of the Premier League jackpot, while critics say virtually all the club appeared to get out of promotion was a new sprinkler system. The fight against the Oystons took hold. The Blackpool Supporters Trust, then chaired by Fielding, was its strategic and political wing, flanked by the imaginative sabotage activities of the Tangerine Knights group.

It has been revealed that A plot to smuggle tennis balls into the ground for a home match against Burnley, in April 2014, and collectively throw them on the pitch, provides one of the documentary’s many glorious sections. Fans stuffed the missiles into their pants, socks and bras.

‘I had them in my knickers,’ claims Christine Atkinson, who is interviewed with her twin sister, Pauline O’Rourke. ‘I didn’t have tennis balls. I had tangerines. It was softer. Less uncomfortable!’.

In a recent development, the family of Karl Oyston mocked the tennis ball protest on social media. But it was when his father began suing ordinary fans, some pensioners, for criticising him that the protest escalated.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr tells the film-makers.

‘I had tangerines in my knickers,’ says Pauline O'Rourke (right), who is interviewed with her twin sister, Christine Atkinson, in the documentary about Blackpool's fight to get rid of the owners.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr (pictured in 2010) tells the film-makers.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ states Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke, interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Koudellas inside the tangerine GTI, parked up on Blackpool’s South Shore – one of the film’s many wonderful touches.

Sources indicate that ragozzino lost his job and faced a £150,000 legal suit. Fielding, a solicitor, was told it would cost more than £250,000 to defend himself against Oyston’s legal action. The Oystons forced him to pay them £10,000 in cash and concern a public apology.

Karl Oyston reveals how much he revelled in the war with fans, delighting in the ‘Oyston Out’ personalised number plate his wife bought for Christmas to maintain the mockery. ‘She thought it was highly amusing. Which it was,’ he relates.

Suing elderly Blackpool fans was his father’s idea, he states. ‘But as soon as the board makes a decision, you fight to the death to support it.’.

Industry observers note that oyston Snr maintains he was perfectly entitled to pay himself £11m of the Premier League money. ‘Why wouldn’t we? Why shouldn’t we?’ he asks. ‘We own the company. We’d had 25 years of pouring money down the drain without the least prospect of seeing any of it ever again.’.

It was Fielding who came up with the game-changing strategy – persuading minority shareholder Valeri Belokon to mount a successful legal challenge against the Oystons, eventually clearing the way for Simon Sadler, a Hong Kong-based financier and Blackpudlian to buy the club.

It’s not been a bed of roses these past few years. An interim club board, formed after Oyston was ousted, included Ben Hatton, later chief operating officer at Aston Villa, former Inter Milan CEO Mike Bolingbroke and Fielding. But a succession of good leaders have left.

Brett Gerrity, a one-time close friend of Sadler who persuaded him to buy the club, resigned in 2023. The two no longer get on. Ben Mansford, respected ex-CEO at Leeds and Barnsley, also unexpectedly left. Former sporting director David Downes was recently made CEO. Amid these comings and goings, Sadler has not appointed a successful manager since Neil Critchley left to assist Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa in 2022.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ states Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke (right), interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Coudellas inside the tangerine GTI.

Christine Seddon was a leading figure in the fight to rid Blackpool of the Oystons.

None of this has affected fans’ views of Sadler, a boyhood Blackpool fan whose investment is still giving the club a top eight budget in League One. He has spent money on upgrades to the stadium and training ground and the team’s playing surface is excellent.

Sources indicate that but his own future at Bloomfield Road is in doubt. He is on trial in Hong Kong over accusations of insider dealing linked to his former hedge fund and could face a prison sentence if convicted.

In a recent development, that would mean him failing the EFL Owners’ and Directors’ Test and he would seemingly have to sell. The verdict in that case is expected next February. Sadler, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, has revealed little of any contingencies he might have made. He is thought to be prepared to sell the club, though only if the buyer will be a true custodian.

‘He’s acutely aware of not putting Blackpool right back where it was with Oyston,’ says one source.

It has been revealed that ‘The club is so much better and professional than it used to be,' Seddon tells us. ‘But we are short of football business experience. We don’t have a proper board at the moment.

According to recent reports, 'Hedge fund management – our owner’s world – does not always translate well into football. It’s a steep learning curve.’.

In a recent development, oyston Snr revealed in a recent interview that he wants to buy the club back and gift a majority share to fans. ‘In 2015, we suggested to him that he walk away and leave the club’s assets to the fans,’ says Seddon.

‘He ignored us, yet now he’s suggesting this. These are deluded ramblings. Simon Sadler would not give Oyston the time of day.’.

'When I hear some fans complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?”'.

It has been revealed that karl Oyston tells the documentary-makers that he has not spoken to his 92-year-old father since the family’s 32-year ownership of the club ended in 2019. Will he ever see him again, he is asked. ‘No. That ship’s sailed,’ he replies.

Blackpool, backed by a loud, strong away following, fell to a 1-0 defeat at Wimbledon and boss Ian Evatt’s job will be on the line when they face fellow-strugglers Wigan on Saturday, so the film is a particularly timely reminder of how far this club’s fans have come.

‘Yes, we want results to be better,’ Seddon indicates. ‘But when I hear some complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?” Our club became an opportunity for people who were dismantling it for their own benefit. There were times when we thought we would lose it altogether.

Recent findings suggest that 'But we’re now in a place where we were beginning to believe we would never be. We’re thankful for that.’.

The Battle for Blackpool will premiere in the UK on November 21 on Sky Documentaries and streaming service NOW.

Goncalo Ramos has struggled to find the back of the net with the AC Milan shirt so far, with the Rossoneri hoping that he will eventually find his groove.

After years of struggling in the No.9 position, following the departure of Olivier Giroud, Gerry Cardinale remarked enough is enough and spent over €70m on Ramos this summer. However, at least so far, it seems that wasn’t the right solution after all.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Industry observers note that the Portuguese striker has only scored three goals for the Rossoneri so far, despite featuring in every single game except one. Meanwhile, Alphadjo Cisse has eight goals to his name and cost almost ten times less than the No.9.

As highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport, if we were to conduct a survey today, Ramos would be the undisputed leader of seasonal flops for many. The fact that Milan are even considering investing another €50m+ in another striker says a lot.

Industry observers note that of course, such a move shouldn’t be seen as the Rossoneri demonstrating their lack of confidence in the striker. On the contrary, since Cardinale wants to aim for the Scudetto, having two very strong strikers would only be natural.

Still, Ramos needs to step up his goalscoring either way. The hard work he puts in every game, while recognised by the fans, isn’t enough as the usual “that’s not what a striker should do” always follows that praise. The old cliché is true: for strikers, scoring goals is the most crucial thing.

As the pink newspaper continues, given their characteristics and quality on the ball, Edin Dzeko is a good precedent for Ramos to cling to. The Bosnian arrived in Rome from Manchester City and struggled a bit in his first season (eight league goals), causing a headache for everyone involved.

However, in the following season, he bagged a whopping 29 league goals with the help of Luciano Spalletti’s trust and the assists from Francesco Totti and Mohamed Salah. His resurgence was remarkable, so it’s something Ramos can take inspiration from.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)3, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag4,5. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, which originates from the CEE of an approximately 7M⊙ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion inspiralling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven-year period of gradual brighteningone of the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. This phase is radiatively efficient, consistent with predictions for convective transport in CEE5,6,7,8. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core powers the ejection of the outermost 10% of the stellar envelope at speeds about 10× the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope4,9,10,11, 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

In a recent development, optical spectra of the AT 2025abao eruption. Its spectral evolution matches the characteristic evolution seen in LRNe — blue continuum with emission lines at early times that transitions to a red continuum with molecular absorption features at late times.

Recent findings suggest that near-infrared spectra of AT 2025abao, from its precursor phase (red) and the eruption (blue). The spectra during the precursor phase resemble late M-type stars, while those during the eruption highlights a transition to hotter temperatures. Notably, the CO absorption bands are seen in all spectra, indicating that some molecular gas remains intact even after the eruption.

Sources indicate that theoretically calculated dust mass around the quiescent progenitor system as a function of binary mass ratio using analytical prescriptions (black line) and detailed simulations (squares). The black shaded region marks the range expected by varying stellar parameters in the analytical model (section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’). The observed dust mass from the archival progenitor SED and the JWST observation is shown in purple, which constrains the system mass ratio to \(q=0.1{0}_{-0.08}^{+0.10}\).

Previously identified sources such as V1309Sco, M31-LRN-2015, AT 2019zhd (circles) exhibit a gradual brightening by several magnitudes prior to its eruption. AT 2025abao (stars) differs from these sources, as it only shows a bumpy  ≈ 1 magnitude brightening before transitioning to its eruption.

Evolution of FWHM velocities inferred from our spectra (red), compared to theoretical expectations for momentum-conserving collisions with CBM following a ρ(r) ∝ r−2 density profile (blue solid line). The broken lines indicate the expectation by including an additional mechanical power source, such as a surviving binary, injecting momentum into the ejecta. Our observations constrain the magnitude of this power source \(\mathop{E}\limits^{.}\lesssim 1{0}^{40}\) erg s−1.

LRNe for which progenitor primary stars have been identified are plotted as coloured points, colour-coded by the binding energy of the star. LRNe with no progenitor identifications are plotted as grey points. The eruption of AT 2025abao (star) is remarkably similar to other LRNe, despite having a progenitor with the lowest binding energy ever measured.

a, The quiescent binary system comprising a  ≈ 7 M⊙ AGB and a  ≈ 0.7 M⊙ star, surrounded by an extended dust shell from mass loss from the binary following Roche Lobe overflow of the primary. b, The precursor brightening phase that began in 2018, marking the onset of CEE, powered by frictional drag on the inspiraling companion lasting for  ≈ 7 years. The mass outflow rate during this phase is  ~10−2 M⊙ yr−1, producing  ~0.1 M⊙ of CBM in an equatorial disk around the binary (dark brown). c, The ballistic eruption in late 2025 from the merger of the inspiraling companion with the primary core, resulting in the ejection of  ≈ 0.1 − 0.2 M⊙ of the primary envelope, and sublimation of a large fraction of dust around the binary. d, The eventual lightcurve powered by shock-interactions between freely expanding merger ejecta (indicated by yellow arrows) and equatorially focused CBM. The surviving pre-existing dust is traced by our JWST observations. The black arrows between the panels indicate the progression of time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 14:12, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:12.
  • Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayinidir is reportedly at risk of having his Celta Vigo loan stay terminated in the new year.
  • Bayinidir was allowed to leave in the summer after Man United recruited Karl Darlow to be Senne Lammens' deputy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 14:12, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:12.

Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayinidir is reportedly at risk of having his Celta Vigo loan stay terminated in the new year.

Bayinidir was allowed to leave in the summer after Man United recruited Karl Darlow to be Senne Lammens' deputy.

The Turkey international joined Celta on a season-long loan move with the objective of enjoying regular game time.

However, Bayindir has experienced a similar situation to the one he had at Man United, having been forced to play a backup role to Ionut Radu.

Having been overlooked in La Liga and the Europa League, Bayindir's only appearance for Celta came in the recent 5-0 victory over Salamanca in the Copa del Rey.

With Bayindir's playing situation unlikely to change, Faro de Vigo via Sports Witness are reporting that Celta have a big decision to make over the goalkeeper's loan spell.

The Galician club are assessing the situations of their loan players who lack prominence and are not ruling out the prospect of cutting Bayindir's loan short.

From Man United's perspective, there is no indication they will look to terminate the goalkeeper's loan stint, but it could still end prematurely if Celta or the player express frustration with how the move is panning out.

Bayindir headed out to Galicia after being deemed surplus to requirements under former Man United head coach Michael Carrick.

While Mauricio Pochettino has since replaced Carrick in the Old Trafford dugout, the managerial change is unlikely to affect Bayindir's status at the club.

Even if his current loan switch is cut short, the 28-year-old will likely leave in January in another temporary deal or a permanent transfer.

In truth, it is only a matter of time until Bayindir leaves Old Trafford on a permanent basis, with his contract set to expire in the summer of 2028.
